Question: Hexadecimal (base-\(16\)) numbers are written using numeric digits \(0\) through \(9\) as well as the letters \(A\) through \(F\) to represent \(10\) through \(15.\) Among the first \(1000\) positive integers, there are \(n\) whose hexadecimal representation contains only numeric digits. What is the sum of the digits of \(n?\)
Solution:
Using leading zeros lets us count short hexadecimal representations together. Since \(16^2=256\) and \(4\cdot256=1024>1000\), every integer under consideration has at most three hexadecimal digits, and its first digit after padding to three positions is at most \(3\).

For a representation containing only numeric digits, the first position therefore has four choices, \(0,1,2,3\), and each remaining position has ten choices, \(0\) through \(9\). Every such string is within the upper bound: the largest is
\[
(399)_{16}=3\cdot256+9\cdot16+9=921<1000.
\]
Thus no additional cutoff cases need to be removed.

Each integer has exactly one three-position representation, so the product \(4\cdot10\cdot10\) counts each eligible integer once. Removing \(000\), which represents zero, gives
\[
n=4\cdot10\cdot10-1=399.
\]
The requested digit sum is \(3+9+9=\boxed{21}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
